title: Polynomial-time approximation threshold for bimatrix Nash equilibria
short_statement: A 2026 preprint claims additive Nash error $0.30954+\delta$ for general bimatrix games, improving the published $1/3+\delta$ benchmark; the exact threshold remains open.
full_statement: In a two-player normal-form game, the row player has payoff matrix $A\in[0,1]^{m\times n}$ and the column player has payoff matrix $B\in[0,1]^{m\times n}$. A mixed strategy profile $(x,y)$ is an $\varepsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium if no player can improve expected payoff by more than $\varepsilon$ through a unilateral deviation: $$\max_i e_i^T A y - x^T A y \le \varepsilon,\qquad \max_j x^T B e_j - x^T B y \le \varepsilon.$$ Exact equilibrium exists by Nash's theorem but is PPAD-complete to compute. The open problem is to determine the best additive approximation guarantee achievable in polynomial time for arbitrary bimatrix games. Deligkas, Fasoulakis, and Markakis give a polynomial-time algorithm for $(1/3+\delta)$-approximate Nash equilibria for every constant $\delta>0$. Rubinstein proves quasi-polynomial lower bounds for some positive constant $\varepsilon$ under a PPAD-ETH assumption, but the constant is far below $1/3$ and does not identify the algorithmic threshold. The historical below-$1/3$ target was either to compute $(1/3-\eta)$-approximate equilibria in polynomial time for some universal $\eta>0$, or to prove hardness for approximation at or near the $1/3$ frontier. Dongchen Li and Hanyu Li's October 2026 preprint, Theorem 1, claims an $(r_*+\delta)$-approximate Nash equilibrium for arbitrary bimatrix payoffs in $[0,1]$, where $r_*\approx0.30954$, in time polynomial in input length and $1/\delta$. This claims to cross $1/3$, but does not settle the exact threshold.
open_problem: Determine the exact polynomial-time additive-Nash threshold; verify or improve the new $0.30954+\delta$ preprint guarantee.
background: Bimatrix games are one of the cleanest mathematical models of strategic interaction in economics. They are also a central source problem for PPAD, the complexity class that captures total search problems proved total by parity or fixed-point arguments. Exact Nash equilibrium computation is hard, so approximation became the practical and theoretical fallback. The approximation question is subtle because coarse constant approximations are easy, quasi-polynomial algorithms can achieve arbitrarily small constant error, and PPAD lower bounds become much stronger when the allowed running time is quasi-polynomial rather than polynomial. The historical $1/3$ barrier is important because it is a concrete, model-independent number in the simplest two-player setting. Moving it in either direction would sharpen the computational meaning of Nash equilibrium: either general games admit better polynomial-time strategic predictions than currently known, or the hardness of equilibrium appears already at a visible constant. A new preprint claims to cross it; the overall quantitative threshold is still unresolved.
known_results: Daskalakis, Goldberg, and Papadimitriou and independently Chen, Deng, and Teng established PPAD-completeness for exact Nash equilibrium computation, including the two-player case. Lipton, Markakis, and Mehta showed that $\varepsilon$-approximate equilibria can be found in quasi-polynomial time by enumerating small supports. Tsaknakis and Spirakis gave a long-standing polynomial-time algorithm with guarantee about $0.3393+\delta$. Deligkas, Fasoulakis, and Markakis improved this to $1/3+\delta$ in polynomial time by refining the descent framework and using a richer set of candidate strategies. On the hardness side, Rubinstein proves that, assuming PPAD-ETH, there is a constant $\varepsilon>0$ for which computing an $\varepsilon$-approximate equilibrium requires quasi-polynomial time. This matches the qualitative quasi-polynomial upper bound, but the hard constant is not known to approach $1/3$. Thus the open part remains the quantitative polynomial-time threshold. Dongchen Li and Hanyu Li's October 2026 preprint, Theorem 1, claims an $(r_*+\delta)$-approximate Nash equilibrium for arbitrary bimatrix payoffs in $[0,1]$, where $r_*\approx0.30954$, in time polynomial in input length and $1/\delta$. This audit has not independently verified the proof.

counterexample_rationale: Finite bimatrix games can refute proposed algorithms, descent lemmas, support-size claims, or factor-revealing inequalities. Hardness proofs require reductions, but small games are useful for discovering barriers.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can optimize payoff matrices against candidate algorithms and identify bottleneck games near the $1/3$ boundary.

literature.synthesis: Approximate Nash computation has two different frontiers. The quasi-polynomial frontier is nearly understood: small-support enumeration gives an $n^{O(\log n)}$ algorithm for any fixed error, and Rubinstein gives matching quasi-polynomial lower bounds for some constant error under PPAD-ETH. The polynomial-time frontier is much sharper numerically and much less understood. The Tsaknakis-Spirakis descent framework dominated for years at $0.3393+\delta$, and Deligkas-Fasoulakis-Markakis pushed it to $1/3+\delta$. A further improvement likely needs either a new structural theorem about approximate best responses in arbitrary bimatrix games or a stronger bottleneck analysis of descent-style methods. A hardness result near $1/3$ would require reductions that preserve a much larger approximation constant than current PPAD-hardness technology provides. The new preprint claims a further descent-framework improvement. Do not confuse this general-game result with stronger guarantees restricted to symmetric games.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Verify the 2026 descent analysis and its worst-case constant before treating it as an established benchmark. Search for worst-case games for the $1/3$ algorithm; formulate candidate improvements as nonconvex optimization or sum-of-squares certificates; revisit support-enumeration and regret-minimization hybrids; study whether Rubinstein-style gadgets can preserve larger additive regret gaps.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A claimed algorithmic result must be polynomial in the matrix dimensions for every payoff pair in $[0,1]$ and must output a profile whose unilateral regrets are bounded by the stated $\varepsilon$. The proof should use additive regret, not multiplicative approximation or well-supported equilibrium unless it explicitly translates the guarantee. A claimed lower bound must state the complexity assumption and the additive approximation constant. Empirical game-search evidence is not a proof, but it can support counterexamples to specific algorithms if the payoff matrices, mixed strategies, best-response values, and exact regret calculations are supplied.
